fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Reading the Sky as Scripture", "body": "Chance describes astrotheology as the scripture in the stars, borrowing Marty Leeds's phrase, and argues the sky itself is a text rather than a place where myths were stored for safekeeping. Multilingual priests and poets read stories out of constellations and star names, leaning heavily on wordplay and punning. His favorite example is Samson, whose name he ties to Shemesh, the sun, and whose jawbone miracle John McHugh traced to a single patch of sky. Chance says astrotheology does not debunk Christianity but shows it is bigger than taught, and that faith strengthened by knowledge is a hardier faith."}, {"title": "Why Religion Keeps a Devil Around", "body": "Dawn opens the devil discussion by quoting Reverend Robert Taylor: if there be no devil there be no saviour. Chance traces the idea back to original sin, which he calls the worst priest jive ever implanted in mankind, and cites Godfrey Higgins calling the devil the grand ally of priests. He compares it to governments inventing boogeymen overseas. Turning to language, he reads diabolos as Lord God or Lord of the Day rather than slanderer, notes Taylor's view of the devil as the sign opposite the sun, and finds father, lord and savior roots in Abaddon, Apollyon and Saturn."}, {"title": "The Serpent and the Morning Star", "body": "Chance argues the Genesis serpent was not originally meant to be the devil. Irenaeus wrote against the Ophites, a sect named for ophis, the Greek serpent, a sound Chance hears inside Sophia, wisdom. The Hebrew word for the serpent can mean subtle or naked, which he reads as sexual symbolism: without that spark, Adam and Eve would sit unchanged in the garden forever, which he equates with death. He also points to Moses raising a brazen serpent that heals, the cloven tongues in Acts, and Jesus calling himself the bright and morning star, the same Venus named Lucifer."}, {"title": "Good and Bad in Everything", "body": "Chance reads the riddle of Epicurus: if God is willing but unable to prevent evil, able but unwilling, or neither, what follows? Dawn answers with duality, describing this realm as experiential, a place where hard experiences let people grow and balance means harmony rather than cancellation. Chance tells her she just answered Epicurus, arguing that what seems evil leads to growth, the way winter clears room for new life, while granting that real malevolence exists. He sees the full spectrum of good and bad in everyone, and says accepting that stops him from idolizing or demonizing people."}, {"title": "Discernment Without Dogma", "body": "Chance and Dawn both warn against turning inspiration into dogma. Chance offers firmament as permanent mind as a personal revelation that can start a trail of research but should never be enforced on anyone, a habit he says runs rampant in Trust Me Bro truther podcasts. He says a contrarian idea is not right just because it opposes the mainstream, and explains why hosting guests is a dance. Dawn, whose show is named for discernment, describes holding two ideas without adopting either. In tuning sessions Chance sees the cost of rigid belief, like a client whose ankle carried contradictory lessons from the book of Job."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: What does the Devil represent in astrotheology? Is there a secret to the serpent of Genesis that tells a Gnostic story? "The Devil is the grand ally of priests. No Devil, no priests." These words were written by Godfrey Higgins in the 19th century, and truer have never been spoken.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In this episode, I join Dawn Lester on her podcast Dawn of Discernment to talk about a nice variety of topics, always circling around to the scripture in the stars, and how to be open to new interpretations of things without getting carried away into new dogmas.
